title: Stack & Queue
tagline: LIFO and FIFO — and the monotonic-stack trick that beats every "next greater element" question.
intro:
Stacks and queues are the two simplest 'ordered access' structures, and the order they enforce is the whole point. A **stack** is LIFO — last in, first out — perfect for anything with nesting or 'most recent' semantics (matching brackets, undo, call stacks, DFS). A **queue** is FIFO — first in, first out — perfect for processing things in arrival order (BFS, scheduling, streaming).

The interview multiplier is the **monotonic stack**: a stack you keep sorted (increasing or decreasing) by popping elements that violate the order before pushing. It answers a whole class of 'next greater / next smaller / previous greater' questions in O(n) that look O(n²) at first glance — daily temperatures, largest rectangle in histogram, stock span.

This module covers both structures, the bracket-matching template, the monotonic-stack template, and BFS level-order with a queue.
objectives: Choose stack (LIFO) vs queue (FIFO) from the problem's access pattern
Use a stack for bracket matching and expression evaluation
Build a monotonic stack to answer next-greater / next-smaller in O(n)
Use a queue for BFS level-order traversal
State why monotonic-stack problems are O(n) despite the inner pop loop

signals: Matching/nesting: brackets, tags, nested structures → stack
"Next greater / next smaller / previous greater element" → monotonic stack
"Most recent", undo, backtrack to last state → stack
Level-by-level processing, shortest path in unweighted graph → queue (BFS)
antiSignals: Random access by index needed → use an array
Need min/max at any time with arbitrary inserts → heap

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
A stack is a pile of plates: you add to the top and take from the top, so the last plate you put down is the first one you pick up. A queue is a line at a ticket counter: the first person in line is served first. The order each one forces is exactly what makes it handy.

Example (stack): checking brackets in `([])`. Push `(`, then push `[`. Now a `]` arrives - it should close the most recently opened bracket, which is `[`, and it does, so pop it. Then `)` should close `(`, and it does. The stack ends empty, so the string is valid. The 'most recent must close first' rule is pure last-in-first-out.

sections.heading: Stack vs queue — the core contract
sections.body:
| Structure | Order | Add | Remove | Look | Java | Python |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Stack** | LIFO | push | pop (top) | peek | `Deque` (`ArrayDeque`) | `list` (append/pop) |
| **Queue** | FIFO | enqueue | dequeue (front) | peek | `ArrayDeque` / `LinkedList` | `collections.deque` |
| **Deque** | both ends | addFirst/Last | pollFirst/Last | peek | `ArrayDeque` | `collections.deque` |

All operations are O(1). In Java, prefer `ArrayDeque` over the legacy `Stack` class (which is synchronised and slower). In Python, never use `list.pop(0)` for a queue — it's O(n); use `collections.deque` for O(1) pops from the front.

callouts.text: Python `list.pop(0)` (front removal) is O(n) because it shifts every element. Always use `collections.deque` with `popleft()` for an O(1) queue.

sections.heading: Bracket matching with a stack
sections.body: The canonical stack problem. Push every opening bracket; on a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener — if not (or the stack is empty), it's invalid. A valid string ends with an empty stack. This LIFO behaviour mirrors how nesting works: the most recently opened bracket must close first.

sections.heading: The monotonic stack
sections.body:
A monotonic stack keeps its elements in sorted order (say, decreasing). Before pushing a new element, **pop everything smaller** — and for each popped element, the new element is its 'next greater element'. Each element is pushed once and popped once, so despite the inner `while`, the total work is O(n).

Use it for: Daily Temperatures, Next Greater Element, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Trapping Rain Water (stack variant), Stock Span.

codeExamples.label: Daily temperatures (next warmer day)

callouts.text: Decide push/pop direction by what you're looking for: a decreasing stack finds the NEXT GREATER element; an increasing stack finds the NEXT SMALLER. Store indices, not values, when you need distances.

sections.heading: Queues and BFS level-order
sections.body: A queue processes nodes in the order they were discovered, which produces breadth-first, level-by-level traversal. The standard pattern records the queue size at the start of each level, then dequeues exactly that many nodes — cleanly separating levels. This is the backbone of shortest-path-in-unweighted-graph and tree level-order problems.

interviewTalking: Name the access pattern: "This is nesting/most-recent, so a stack (LIFO)." or "This needs level-by-level order, so a queue (BFS)." For next-greater problems, say: "A brute force is O(n²), but a monotonic stack does it in O(n) — I keep a decreasing stack and pop smaller elements as the answer arrives, so each index is pushed and popped once." That amortised O(n) argument is the signal interviewers want.
commonMistakes: Using Python `list.pop(0)` as a queue (O(n)) instead of `deque.popleft()` (O(1))
Using Java's legacy `Stack` class instead of the faster `ArrayDeque`
Popping from an empty stack — always check before pop/peek
Storing values instead of indices in a monotonic stack when distances are needed
Wrong monotonic direction (increasing vs decreasing) for next-greater vs next-smaller
Not capturing `len(queue)` before the level loop in BFS, mixing levels together
complexityNotes: Stack/queue/deque operations are O(1). Bracket matching and monotonic-stack problems are O(n) time, O(n) space — each element is pushed and popped at most once. BFS is O(V + E) time and O(V) space for the queue.
